meaning: The hunter — orisha of the hunt, the forest, and deliberate strategy (standard Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì; Cuban Ochosi, Brazilian Oxóssi)

pronunciation.approximation: aw-shaw-AW-sih — the dotted ọ is the open 'aw' of 'law'; ṣ is 'sh'; the tones run low-high-low-low.
pronunciation.note: The name in standard Yoruba orthography is Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì, fully tone-marked; the owned form Ọṣọọsì keeps the underdotted vowels (ọ, the open o) and the long double-o while following the diaspora convention that leaves tone marks implicit — the spelling carried across the Santería and Candomblé worlds. Abraham's Dictionary of Modern Yoruba lists him as the god of hunters; the etymology is debated, though the ọ̀ṣọ́ element suggests swiftness. Tier-1 by rule: the underdots and the ṣ are distinctive letters the ASCII "Ochosi" cannot carry.

domains.title: The Single Arrow
domains.subtitle: The Hunt, the Forest, and the Justice of the Patient Shot
domains.lead: Ọṣọọsì is the hunter orisha: lord of the forest, master of the bow, and patron of strategy — the one whose praise-poems say he kills with a single arrow, because he has learned what every hunter must learn: wait.

cards.name: The Single Arrow
cards.desc: One shaft, never wasted: his oríkì hail the hunter who does not need to shoot twice.

cards.name: The Bow (Ofá)
cards.desc: His emblem across three continents — the hunter's bow, carved on his shrines and sung in his names.

cards.name: The Forest (Igbó)
cards.desc: His cathedral and his larder: the deep bush where game, medicine, and danger all live.

cards.name: Justice
cards.desc: In the diaspora he stands with the accused: the orisha of right judgment and the patient case.

symbols.name: The bow and arrow
symbols.meaning: Skill married to patience: the whole doctrine of the hunt in one image

symbols.name: The forest
symbols.meaning: The realm of the provider — game, leaves, and the tests that make a tracker

symbols.name: The single shot
symbols.meaning: Strategy as worship: preparation so complete that one attempt suffices

mythology.lead: Ọṣọọsì's mythology lives in praise-poetry and divination verse — the oríkì that greet him, the Ifá corpus that ranks him among the orisha, and the itan, the sacred stories of the diaspora houses that still tell of the one arrow.

myths.title: The Hunter Who Kills Once
myths.text: His praise-poems are the hunt distilled: the oríkì greet Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì as the hunter who kills with a single arrow — the archer whose patience is so complete that the forest gives him what it denies the noisy and the hasty. In the Candomblé houses of Brazil the same idea opens his festivals: Oxóssi, rei das matas, king of the forest, the provider whose one shot feeds the whole town. The oríkì tradition is not ornament here; it is the liturgy of competence.

myths.title: The Orisha of the Odù
myths.text: In the Ifá divination corpus — the 256 odù and their thousands of memorized verses — the divine hunter walks as provider and strategist: the orisha who knows the paths of the bush as the babaláwo knows the paths of the palm nuts. Bascom's fieldwork in Ife and among Cuban practitioners recorded his place in the diviners' world; Idowu's theology of the orisha sets him among the ministers Olódùmarè appointed over creation's wild half. Wherever Ifá is consulted, the forest has a spokesman.

myths.title: Among the Warriors
myths.text: In Cuban Santería, Ochosi stands with the Guerreros — the Warriors: Eleguá who opens the road, Ogún who clears it with iron, Ochosi who hunts its game, and Osún who keeps watch — the first orishas a practitioner receives. His Cuban face is the justice-bringer: devotees call on him in court cases and wrongful accusations, the hunter whose arrow finds the truth the way it finds the heart of the deer. The hunt and the lawsuit are one skill: tracking.

myths.title: Oxóssi of the Twentieth of January
myths.text: In Brazil, Oxóssi was paired with São Sebastião — the Roman soldier shot through with arrows for refusing to renounce his faith, his iconography a perfect mirror for the archer orisha — and the saint's feast of January 20 became Oxóssi's own. In Umbanda his name heads the whole linha de Oxóssi, the line of the caboclo spirits, the indigenous forest guides. Three nations, three spellings, one bow.

lore.syncretism: The diaspora rebuilt him with local materials and never lost the pattern. Cuba gave him the Guerreros and the courtroom; Brazil gave him São Sebastião's feast-day and the caboclos of Umbanda; Trinidad, Haiti, and the United States received the Lukumí lineages intact. Scholars from Bascom to Verger mapped the route: the Ketu nation's Oxóssi, the Oyo-heritage hunter, and the Yoruba Ọ̀ṣọ́ọ̀sì of Abraham's dictionary are one figure wearing three orthographies. His closest cousins abroad are the other divine hunters — but none of them shoots only once.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ọṣọọsì is a living god, not a memory: his festivals still fill the terreiros of Bahia, his initiates still receive the Guerreros in Havana and Miami, and his oríkì are still sung in the tonal Yoruba that the written restoration tries to honor. The single arrow has become the tradition's own emblem of Afro-diasporic resilience — patience, precision, and provision against every odds. The spelling Ọṣọọsì keeps the marked vowels of the language the praise-poems were made in.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ọṣọọsì teaches the economics of the one shot: that most waste is noise, that readiness looks like stillness, and that the forest feeds the one who has already done the waiting. In an age of volume, he is the orisha of the opposite — the deliberate act, the counted arrow, the case prepared so well it needs to be made only once.

sources.name: Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief

lore.archaeology: The hunter orisha's record is oral and liturgical rather than monumental: his corpus is the Ifá verse tradition, the oríkì preserved by praise-singers, and the ethnographies of Abraham, Idowu, Bascom, and Verger. His material culture is real but perishable — bows, iron implements, and forest shrines — and his oldest durable monuments are the diaspora's: the terreiros of Bahia, some a century and more old, the casa-templos of Havana, and the January streets of Rio on São Sebastião's day.
